title: Average Velocity of Gas Molecules in Kinetic Theory
short_intro: Average velocity in kinetic theory refers to the arithmetic mean of the velocities of all molecules in a given gas mass at thermal equilibrium. Due to random isotropic motion in a stationary container, its vector sum and average magnitude vanish identically, making scalar speeds like root-mean-square and mean speed physically relevant.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of molecular speeds, distinction between average velocity, mean speed, and root-mean-square speed, and dependence on temperature and molar mass.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution function, probability density integration, most probable speed, and relationship between different statistical speeds.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Vector Nature of Average Velocity
bullets: The average velocity vector of gas molecules is defined as the arithmetic mean of the individual velocity vectors: v_av = (1/N) Σ v_i.
In a gas at rest inside a stationary container, molecules move equally in all directions with no net directional flow.
Consequently, the average velocity vector is identically zero: v_av = 0.

concept_notes.heading: Distinction Between Average Velocity and Mean Speed
bullets: While average velocity considers directional vectors, mean speed (or average speed) considers the scalar magnitudes of velocities.
Mean speed v_bar = (1/N) Σ |v_i| is non-zero and always positive.
Mean speed is derived by integrating the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution function from zero to infinity.

concept_notes.heading: Dependence on Temperature and Molecular Mass
bullets: Characteristic speeds of gas molecules depend directly on the absolute temperature T.
Characteristic speeds vary inversely with the square root of the molar mass M or molecular mass m.
Heavier gases possess lower average speeds compared to lighter gases at the same thermodynamic temperature.

concept_notes.heading: Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution Overview
bullets: The distribution gives the fraction of molecules having speeds in the range between v and v + dv.
It incorporates three characteristic speeds: most probable speed (v_mp), mean speed (v_bar), and root-mean-square speed (v_rms).
The hierarchy of these speeds is always v_mp < v_bar < v_rms for any ideal gas at absolute temperature T.

derivations.title: Derivation of Mean Speed from Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas in thermal equilibrium obeying Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics
steps: Write the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution function for molecular speeds: dn/n = 4π (m / 2πkT)^(3/2) v^2 exp(-mv^2 / 2kT) dv.
Set up the integral for mean speed: v_bar = ∫ v (dn/n) from v = 0 to v = ∞.
Evaluate the definite standard integral: ∫ v^3 exp(-mv^2 / 2kT) dv = (2kT/m)^2.
Substitute the evaluated integral back into the expression and simplify constants.

derivations.title: Derivation of Root-Mean-Square Speed
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas obeying classical kinetic theory assumptions
steps: Start from the kinetic pressure equation of an ideal gas: P = (1/3) ρ v_{rms}^2.
Substitute the ideal gas law in terms of density: P = (ρRT) / M.
Equate the two expressions for pressure: (1/3) ρ v_{rms}^2 = (ρRT) / M.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Asymmetric bell-shaped curve of fraction of molecules versus molecular speed, marking v_mp, v_bar, and v_{rms}.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that very slow and very high speeds are rare, with the peak representing the most probable speed.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT multiple-choice questions regarding the relative positions of v_mp, v_bar, and v_{rms}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effect of Temperature on Speed Distribution
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two curves on the same axes: one at lower temperature T_1 (taller peak, shifted left) and higher temperature T_2 (broader, flatter peak, shifted right).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Higher temperature increases the spread of speeds and shifts the peak to a higher velocity value while maintaining equal total area under the curve.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct conceptual questions on how heating alters molecular speed distribution.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effect of Molar Mass on Speed Distribution
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves for a heavy gas (like CO_2) and a light gas (like H_2) at the same temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Lighter gas curve peaks at a higher speed with a wider spread; heavier gas curve is sharper and shifted toward lower speeds.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Comparative analysis questions in TGT and PGT examinations.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of hydrogen molecules at 300 K. Take R = 8.314 J mol^{-1} K^{-1} and M = 2 x 10^{-3} kg mol^{-1}.
solution_steps: Substitute values: R = 8.314, T = 300, M = 2 x 10^{-3}.

solved_numericals.question: At what temperature will the root-mean-square speed of oxygen molecules (M = 32 g mol^{-1}) be equal to the root-mean-square speed of helium molecules (M = 4 g mol^{-1}) at -73 °C?
solution_steps: Convert helium temperature to Kelvin: T_{He} = -73 + 273 = 200 K.
Solve for T_{O2}: T_{O2} = T_{He} \times (M_{O2} / M_{He}) = 200 \times (32 / 4) = 200 \times 8 = 1600 K.

solved_numericals.question: For a gas obeying Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, find the ratio of the mean speed to the root-mean-square speed.
solution_steps: Recall expression for mean speed: v_{bar} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}.
Recall expression for root-mean-square speed: v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Molecules are treated as point masses interacting solely via elastic collisions, ignoring intermolecular forces except during collisions.
The gas is dilute and behaves ideally, obeying PV = nRT.
Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution assumes thermodynamic equilibrium and a large number of molecules, failing at extremely low temperatures or high quantum densities.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The average velocity of gas molecules is equal to the mean speed.
common_misconceptions.correct: Average velocity is zero for a stationary gas, whereas mean speed is a positive scalar quantity.
common_misconceptions.why: Velocity is a vector quantity, and random motion in all directions causes vector cancellation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All molecules in a gas at temperature T move at the same speed.
common_misconceptions.correct: Molecules possess a wide continuous range of speeds governed by the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal collisions constantly redistribute kinetic energy among individual molecules.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Root-mean-square speed is the arithmetic average of molecular speeds.
common_misconceptions.correct: RMS speed is the square root of the average of squared speeds, giving higher weight to faster molecules.
common_misconceptions.why: The mathematical definition involves squaring speeds before averaging, unlike the simple arithmetic mean speed.

quick_revision: Average velocity of a confined gas is always zero due to random isotropic motion.
Mean speed is given by \sqrt{8RT / \pi M}.
Root-mean-square speed is given by \sqrt{3RT / M}.
Most probable speed is given by \sqrt{2RT / M}.
All characteristic molecular speeds are directly proportional to the square root of absolute temperature and inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass.
